items.title: Java4Shell: GitLab helps find and remediate a critical Java flaw
items.summary: GitLab has internally assessed the impact of Java4Shell, and concluded it is not exploitable in GitLab-managed infrastructure. Exploitation requires a specific combination of conditions, which we confirmed are not present in our production environment. A single component was found to contain the impacted bundle in its runtime environment, which we are proactively upgrading as a hardening measure.On November 17, 2026, OpenJDK, the project that most Java runtimes are built from, fixed a memory corruption flaw known as Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938, CVSS 8.1) in the optimized java.util.Base64 decoding used on recent x86-64 CPUs. Web servers and frameworks routinely decode Base64 values from users, such as authentication headers and cookies, before the application sees the request. Researchers have demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution in the default configurations of several widely used Java products.Upgrade Java to a fixed version nowTo mitigate this issue, upgrade every Java runtime from 17.0.6 onward, including unsupported releases such as Java 18 and 24, to a build based on OpenJDK 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, or 27.0.1.1, or to your distribution’s patched package. If you can’t upgrade right away, turn off the vulnerable optimization with the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics JVM option.Here are fixed builds and packages as of November 19:Vendor or distributionFixed build or packageOpenJDK17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1Eclipse Temurin17.0.21.1+2, 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2, 27.0.1.1+4Amazon Corretto17.0.21.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2, 25.0.5.1.2, 27.0.1.1.4Azul Zulu17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1BellSoft Liberica17.0.21.1+5, 21.0.13.1+5, 25.0.5.1+5, 27.0.1.1+5SapMachine17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1Microsoft Build of OpenJDK17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1Oracle Java SE 8 Performance Pack8u513-perf. Other Java 8 builds aren’t affectedUbuntu 26.10, 26.04, 24.04, 22.04openjdk-17 17.0.21.1, openjdk-21 21.0.13.1, openjdk-25 25.0.5.1, and on 26.10 openjdk-27 27.0.1.1Ubuntu 20.04 and 18.04 (ESM)openjdk-17 17.0.21.1, and on 20.04 openjdk-21 21.0.13.1Debian 13 and 12Fixed only in unstable for nowAlpine 3.24 and 3.23openjdk17 17.0.21.1, openjdk21 21.0.13.1, openjdk25 25.0.5.1Alpine 3.22No fix, as its openjdk packages are no longer supportedAmazon Linux 2023The Corretto versions above, as java-17, java-21, java-25, and java-27-amazon-correttoRHEL 10, 9, and 8No fix yetSources: the OpenJDK advisory, vendors’ release pages, and the Ubuntu, Debian, Alpine, and Red Hat security trackers, as of November 19, 2026.How you apply the upgrade depends on where Java runs:Containers with a floating tag, such as amazoncorretto:21: Rebuild the image so it pulls the latest base image, then redeploy.Containers with a pinned tag: Change the tag to a fixed version, then redeploy.Hosts: Upgrade the package, then restart every Java process.For containers, check that the new base image ships a fixed version. As of November 19, eclipse-temurin:21 and the images built on it, such as tomcat, still don't, so they need the workaround below until they do.If you can’t upgrade yet, turn off the vulnerable optimizationSet the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics JVM option, and restart every Java process for it to take effect. Base64 decoding will then use the regular version, which doesn’t have the flaw, and is only slightly slower.To apply it to every JVM a container starts, add it to the JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS environment variable, keeping any value already set. In a shell script, such as the container’s entrypoint, add this line of code:export JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="${JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS:+$JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS }-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics"To confirm the option is set, run java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics in the container, which should print false.Locate Java projects across your GitLab groupsAny project that runs Java needs a fixed version, including the ones that are easy to forget, such as a CI tool, a build server, or a product that bundles its own JDK. Finding them takes two views: a static search of what your repositories declare and your images contain, and a runtime inventory of what actually runs. GitLab covers the static view with three features: container scanning, GitLab Orbit, and a language filter. Use them in this order.1. Container scanningContainer scanning reports vulnerabilities in operating system packages, so it finds Java installed with apt, apk, or dnf. It reports the CVE once the CVE reaches the advisories in the scanner’s vulnerability database. To turn it on for a project, add the template to .gitlab-ci.yml:include:    - template: Security/Container-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml     container_scanning:    variables:      # Experimental, Ultimate only: also reports runtimes not installed by a package manager      CS_BINARY_SCAN: "true"You can also use a group-level scan execution policy to turn container scanning on for every project in a group at once.
